title: Study Abroad Experience at the University of Pennsylvania
paragraphs: From late March to the end of May, I studied abroad at the University of Pennsylvania in the United States. The University of Pennsylvania is one of the world's leading universities and belongs to the Ivy League, the association of prestigious private universities on the US East Coast. Although two months is a short period, it was a good experience to be able to study in such an environment.

For four weeks from March 28, I did a clerkship in pediatric cardiology at CHOP (Children's Hospital of Philadelphia). The four-week schedule was two weeks on the ward, one week in the outpatient clinic and one week on consults. On the morning of the first day of the clerkship, I went to the department office in CHOP designated by email, exchanged a few words with the administrative staff, was taken by that person to the ward, and was abruptly thrown into the morning rounds of pediatric cardiology. And the attending there suddenly said to me, "Explain what you know about aortic stenosis," and I stammered. Somehow I followed the morning rounds, and when I thought they had ended, everyone began to go about their own duties, and I was left more or less abandoned. It was completely different from the situation, always scheduled, that I had experienced in Polyclinic 1 in Japan, and thrown into a space of a foreign language, even though I could speak it to a certain extent, my morale was considerably worn down. I regretted that I had not been prepared enough and had not done enough preparation. I gradually learned as I did clerkships in the United States, but if students do not go forward aggressively on their own, they are left alone. There is no atmosphere that tolerates the passive; leniency is shown only to those who study and take part actively. From the second day of the clerkship, I established a style of asking nearby staff questions when there was something I did not understand on the morning rounds, and catching the fellow to follow up when the rounds were over. In the outpatient week and the consult week too, I asked questions actively about things I did not understand and tried to join in as much as possible even in small matters such as everyday conversation. It was a good experience to see rare congenital heart diseases that one can hardly see in the pediatrics department at Nagoya University, such as tetralogy of Fallot, TAPVR and aortic stenosis. In addition, in the pediatric cardiology rotation, one is given the assignment of choosing a pediatric cardiology disease at some point in the four weeks and giving a presentation of 30 to 40 minutes. I had quite a hard time searching for the literature, but I remember that when I finished, the doctor said "good job," and I patted my chest in relief.

In the second month I was allowed to rotate through hematology/oncology at Pennsylvania Hospital. In this department, unlike the first month, which was mainly observation, it was a parade of hands-on work. By chance, I was to rotate through this department together with 濱田, who had come from Nagoya University with me, and the system in this department was that the students make the first contact for hematology/oncology consults. We left our phone numbers at the desk and observed the outpatient clinic until a consult came in from another department. When a consult came, the desk phoned us, and we slipped out of the outpatient clinic, went to the ward, and read through the chart. Once we had obtained the reason for the consult and general information about the patient, the flow was that we examined the patient ourselves, summarized the necessary information, wrote the assessment and plan, presented to the attending, and then went to see the patient with the attending. At first there were difficulties, such as not knowing which part of the chart had the necessary information, but I felt as if we were part of the cycle of care, and I remember it was a very enjoyable month. Also, Pennsylvania Hospital is the oldest hospital in the United States, and part of it was like a museum. The oldest operating table in the United States was on display and I could enter a library where old documents were preserved, so I was also able to feel Philadelphia, which has a long history even within the United States.

Aspects other than the clerkship were also quite fulfilling. I lived for two months at a place called the International House of Philadelphia, which the seniors who had studied abroad at Penn had also used. Although the quality of the accommodation was not worth the price, as its name says it is accommodation for overseas students coming to study in Philadelphia, and parties and the like were held from time to time, so just by spending time there I could make a great many friends. In my free time I really had a wonderful time, going drinking with those friends or going to New York to play. At the end they even held a farewell party, and I think I made friends I want to stay connected with for life. I strongly hope that juniors who go to Penn in the future will use this facility. Also, unlike the other American universities that Nagoya University students can study at, Penn is located in a city, so it was good that I could enjoy American urban life. On the occasional days when the clerkship ended early, I used the happy hour to have a drink, which was a lot of fun.

I am really glad I went abroad. I was painfully made aware of how narrow a world I had been living in and how passively I had learned until now. The American healthcare system, the atmosphere inside actual hospitals and the students' attitudes were all different from Japan, and I feel that by going to the United States I was able to pry open the values that had been closed until then. It is not a matter of which is better; my horizons were greatly broadened. Of course one can learn actively even in Japan, and I know many Nagoya University students who do. But in my case, since entering medical school I had also been immersed in the lukewarmness peculiar to Japanese university students, and I felt that this study abroad woke me up in that respect. A situation in which, unless you learn and seek on your own, you are left alone. For me, who will become a working adult from now on, it seems to have been very good medicine.

I would like to take this opportunity to express my gratitude. Thank you very much to everyone at the International Collaboration Office and the Academic Affairs staff, starting with Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川 and Ms. 西尾, who made great efforts to make this study abroad possible. I also thank my parents who supported me financially. Thank you. Finally, I would like to end this account by expressing my thanks to my friends in Japan who celebrated my return and to 濱田, who studied abroad with me.
